typologies.title: Structured transfers below a reporting threshold
typologies.question: Were several transfers sized to stay under a threshold rather than sized by need?
counter_evidence: A payroll, rent or instalment schedule can produce similar amounts on a regular cadence.
Per-transfer limits set by the business's own bank or the channel can cap amounts without any intent to avoid a threshold.
Check whether the same pattern is present in the months before the alert window; a long-standing habit is weaker evidence than a new one.

typologies.title: Funds forwarded cross-border shortly after arriving
typologies.question: Did this account hold the money, or only pass it on?
counter_evidence: Treasury sweeps, supplier settlement and payroll runs are all fast by design.
A named, consistent counterparty on both legs is a weaker signal than a new one.
A corridor entity funded by its parent and paying suppliers the same week is the ordinary shape of this business, not a pass-through.

typologies.title: Many unrelated senders paying one account
typologies.question: Why are these particular senders all paying the same account?
counter_evidence: A marketplace, a collection agent or a group treasury account receives from many unrelated parties by design.
Check whether the senders are this entity's own customers — many-to-one is the normal shape of a collection account.
A rising sender count that tracks a product launch is growth, not a funnel.

typologies.title: Funds returning to their origin through intermediaries
typologies.question: Did this money travel, or only appear to?
counter_evidence: Intra-group treasury movements legitimately return to the parent; check whether every account on the path belongs to the same group.
A refund or a reversed payment returns money by design — check whether a leg carries a reversal reference.
Trade finance and back-to-back invoicing can produce a genuine loop.

typologies.title: Activity far above, or beside, what the entity declared
typologies.question: Does this account behave like what the business said it was for?
counter_evidence: A seasonal peak or a single large contract can lift a month far above the declared average without changing what the business does.
The declared expectation was given at onboarding and may simply be stale — check when the KYB evidence was last refreshed.
An off-profile purpose code may be a coding error at the payer's end rather than a change in activity.

typologies.title: Transfers that cannot be judged because information is absent
typologies.question: Can we say who is on both ends of this money, and why it moved?
counter_evidence: A field absent from the feed is not the same as a field the business refused to give — check whether the channel carries it at all.
Ownership may be on file in the KYB pack and simply not linked to these transfers.
This typology is a reason a case cannot be decided yet, not evidence of wrongdoing.

rules.title: A payment for this business instruction already exists
rules.reason: The same purchase order or instruction identifier was submitted again. The engine returned the first payment rather than creating a second one; this rule records that it happened, because a retry loop is worth knowing about.

rules.title: Same amount to the same supplier inside 24 hours
rules.reason: Two payments of the same amount to the same beneficiary under different instruction identifiers. Idempotency cannot catch this one — the instruction identifiers differ — so it is a question for a person.

rules.title: The provider feed sent events this payment could not accept
rules.reason: One or more events were illegal for the state the payment was in and were quarantined. The ledger is intact; the upstream feed is not.

rules.title: The ledger and the provider disagree about what moved
rules.reason: What the product's own books say left the business does not equal the gross the provider reports. Someone is short, and it is either the business or the book.

rules.title: Payout velocity far above this business's own baseline
rules.reason: More payments in the window than this business's own history supports. Busy is not suspicious; busy *for this payer* is worth a look.

rules.title: Amount far above this business's usual payment
rules.reason: The payment is several times the business's typical ticket. Large is not suspicious; large for this payer is.

rules.title: Repeated identical round amounts to one supplier
rules.reason: Invoices rarely land on the same round figure twice. A repeated round amount is either a standing arrangement — which the contract will show — or it is not invoice-driven at all.

rules.title: The supplier's bank account changed recently
rules.reason: Business email compromise works by changing where the money goes. A recent change is the single highest-value fact on this payment.

rules.title: No current independent verification of these bank details
rules.reason: Either the details were never verified, or the verification on file pre-dates the account change — in which case it verified a different account.

rules.title: First payment to this counterparty
rules.reason: No settled payment to this supplier exists yet. Ordinary on its own — every relationship starts once — and it carries weight only in combination.

rules.title: Payment routed to a country the supplier is not registered in
rules.reason: The receiving bank is in a different jurisdiction from the supplier on the contract. There are good reasons for this; none of them are visible from the payment alone.

rules.title: This account receives from several unrelated businesses
rules.reason: Shared payout accounts are not ordinary between unrelated payers. A collection agent and a mule account look identical here, which is exactly why a person decides.

rules.title: Settlement is outside FX tolerance of the booked quote
rules.reason: The amount settled does not follow from the instruction at the rate on file, beyond the 75 basis-point tolerance.

rules.title: Fee does not match the corridor's schedule
rules.reason: The fee charged is not what this corridor and payment size produce.

rules.title: The conversion behind this payment used an expired quote
rules.reason: The quote had expired before it was executed. The rate applied was not a rate the payer was ever shown. The FX desk fails closed on this, so a signal here means the record disagrees with the desk.

rules.title: Purpose code outside the entity's declared activity
rules.reason: The purpose does not belong to what this business said it does. Often a coding error at the payer's end — and sometimes not.

rules.title: Month-to-date payouts far above the declared expectation
rules.reason: The entity is moving several times what it told us at onboarding. The expectation may simply be stale, which is itself a KYB refresh.

rules.title: Required supporting evidence is missing
rules.reason: A document this payment type requires is absent. This is not a risk claim; it is the reason the payment cannot be decided yet.

rules.title: Instruction text contains directions aimed at an automated reader
rules.reason: Supplier-supplied text is attacker-controlled. Text addressing a model rather than a person is treated as an attack surface and quarantined before any AI reads it.

rules.title: Instruction text claims an approval that is not in the system
rules.reason: The note asserts a pre-approval, exception or sign-off. No such record exists, and an assertion in free text is not an authorisation.

rules.title: Instruction text carries a known business-payment risk pattern
rules.reason: Urgency, an executive bypassing the usual channel, settlement moved off the agreed channel, or a payee name that does not match the contract. These are the patterns the intervention ladder was measured on.

dataset.kind: synthetic, seeded, deliberately enriched with planted patterns
dataset.caveat: Every figure here was produced by corridoros.scenario.population. No real business, account, supplier or transfer is involved. The population is deliberately enriched, so recall and precision are both far higher than any real monitoring system would see, and neither transfers to production traffic.

evaluation.boundary: No model participates in detection, deduplication, aggregation or prioritisation. Every alert above is reproducible from the transfer feed alone.

payload.policy: The amount alone warrants a reminder to check the payee against the contract.
payload.why_not_weaker: A weaker level would not address first_payment_to_beneficiary.
payload.why_not_stronger: No deterministic rule supports a stronger intervention from the available inputs.

payload.policy: Stop. A second approver and an independent callback are required before this payment may be submitted.
payload.why_not_weaker: A payee-account change or payee-name mismatch on a payment of this size is pinned to a stop; averaging it against the other inputs is exactly the mistake this rule exists to prevent.
